task.title: Links
task.shortdesc: An XML document can contain text that should point to another document or to a place in the same document. HTML has standard elements and attributes for links. XML can use any element and attribute names, so CSSMedia cannot know which elements are links by looking at their names. Use the CSSMedia -cssmedia-link property to tell it which elements act as links and what destination each one has.

context.p: To write a link rule, first find the relevant element and attribute in your XML. The selector at the start of a rule chooses XML elements. A declaration inside the braces sets a property in the form property: value;. Names such as xref and target below are examples. Replace them with names used in your XML. See Selectors overview for more ways to choose elements.

info.p: The -cssmedia-link property is a CSSMedia extension. It is not a standard CSS property, so its name has the vendor prefix -cssmedia-.
CSSMedia accepts these values:

ul.li: none means the element is not a link. This is the initial value.
One or more <string> values. A string can be a full URL, a relative address, or a fragment such as #details.
One or more <url> values. CSS Values 4 defines <url> as url() or src().

info.p: A <string> is text written between quotation marks, such as "chapter-2.xml#installation". url() and src() are functions that supply a URL value.
Strings and URLs can be mixed in one value. CSSMedia joins them in order without adding spaces or other characters. The joined result is the link destination.
The property is not inherited. Set it on each element that should act as a link. -cssmedia-link: none removes the link from a selected element.
Suppose your XML contains an xref element with a target attribute:
Use the element name in the selector and the attribute name in attr():

xref selects each element named xref. attr(target) reads the value of that element’s target attribute. The quoted text inside the XML element is its display text; the attribute supplies its destination. If the target attribute is missing, attr() supplies an empty string unless you provide a fallback.
A same-document link can use a fragment identifier. This example reads the id attribute from an xref and adds # before it:
The two parts are joined to form #details. The fragment identifies a location in the current XML document.
You can also write a destination directly. This example uses an attribute selector to match an xref whose role attribute is external:

A relative string destination, such as "chapter-2.xml#installation", is resolved against the XML document’s URL. A URL written with url("chapter-2.xml#installation") is resolved against the stylesheet’s URL. Use a quoted string when the address is meant to be relative to the XML document.
src() is also part of the CSS <url> grammar. CSSMedia resolves its URL against the stylesheet URL, like url().
Selectors define these hyperlink pseudo-classes:

ul.li: :any-link selects elements acting as hyperlink sources.
:link selects links. Its visited-state distinction from :visited applies to browsers, not PDF output.

info.p: PDF links have no visited state. CSSMedia treats :link and :any-link identically: both select elements whose -cssmedia-link value is not none. The browser-history pseudo-class :visited is accepted by the selector parser, but never matches.
For example, to set the color of every element that you assigned a destination:
The pseudo-class selects the link. The color declaration sets its text color. Setting the -cssmedia-link property alone does not choose how the link looks.
:local-link selects a link based on how its destination compares with the XML document’s URL.

ul.li: :local-link matches when the destination is the same document URL. CSSMedia removes the fragment identifiers before comparing the URLs. Thus a link to #details is local to the current document.
:local-link(0) matches links with the same URL origin. An origin consists of the URL scheme, host and port.
:local-link(1) matches links with the same origin and first path segment.
:local-link(2) matches links with the same origin and first two path segments. Higher non-negative integers check that many initial path segments.
